headline: New Zealand Parliament’s Final Sitting Puts Grocery Costs, Health and RMA Reforms at Centre of Election Fight
summary: New Zealand’s final parliamentary sitting before the election campaign was dominated by disputes over grocery prices, household finances, public services and the Government’s record. The Government highlighted the passage of major resource-management reforms and progress on health targets, while opposition parties challenged its claims and criticised changes affecting workers, Māori and the environment. MPs also approved new parliamentary rules and heard that the New Zealand-India free-trade agreement had been ratified.

topicSummaries.topic: Grocery Prices Put Supermarket Competition Under Election Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The cost and availability of groceries directly affect household budgets, while any changes to supermarket competition could influence prices over time.
topicSummaries.content: Labour MP Arena Williams pressed Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer on whether shoppers were paying too much and why further action should wait. Brewer acknowledged that grocery prices were too high, saying the Government had strengthened competition settings and commissioned analysis of structural options; he said separating Foodstuffs had the strongest case among those examined. Brewer said the analysis was complete and the Commerce Commission would consider it and make recommendations after the election. Williams challenged the Government over grocery bills and the $274,000 cost of the analysis, while Brewer cited lower annual food inflation than in Labour’s final year in office.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why should a family whose grocery bill is higher today than when National took office believe that their food will be more affordable under that plan, when all along he has been telling us that, under his Government, it will just get more expensive more slowly?

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Brewer (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Because, under this Government, our track record on inflation, food inflation included, stands for itself. In the last 12 months to July 2026, food inflation was just 1.9 percent. In the last 12 months of the previous Labour Government, food inflation for one year was 12.5 percent.

topicSummaries.topic: Cost of Living and Taxes Dominate Final Election-Eve Clash
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The parties’ competing economic plans could affect household purchasing power, employment, wages and public spending after the election.
topicSummaries.content: In the final question time before the election campaign, Labour leader Chris Hipkins challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon over food and electricity prices, unemployment, wages, housing and pay equity. Luxon defended the Government’s record by pointing to economic growth, tax relief and falling inflation, and argued that new taxes would further burden households. In their closing speeches, the Government and opposition also offered sharply different accounts of the economy and public services: Labour raised concerns about job losses, hardship and the reversal of pay-equity changes, while National promoted its record and campaigned on a promise of no new taxes. These were competing political claims, not findings resolved in the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is he still laser-focused on the cost of living, given the price of butter is up 71 percent under his leadership; bread, 65 percent; mince, 36 percent—all prices going up since he became Prime Minister—or does he just say to New Zealanders struggling with the cost of living, as he did in the House last week, “cry me a river”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: No. What I’d say to New Zealanders about the cost of living is that you sure as hell don’t want any tax increases.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Debate Pits Improving Targets Against Pressure on Hospitals
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Emergency-department delays, treatment waiting lists and staffing levels affect people seeking timely care across the country.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown said the latest quarterly figures showed improvement across all five Government health targets for a second consecutive year, including fewer patients waiting more than four months for treatment and shorter waits in several districts. Labour’s Ayesha Verrall challenged him over reported pressure at Middlemore and Christchurch hospitals and a fall in nurse numbers in Waikato. Brown responded with target results for those hospitals and said the Government had added doctors and nurses to the health workforce. He acknowledged that more work remained, while the two sides disputed how the reported improvements should be weighed against hospital capacity concerns.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Can he confirm that in Christchurch emergency department, 15,000 patients were treated in corridors last year, nearly four times more than in 2023?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We’ve got more good news, and if you look at the most recent health targets report, shorter wait-times for elective treatment at Canterbury has improved from 62.9 percent of patients seen within four months, up to 71.4 percent seen within four months.

topicSummaries.topic: RMA Replaced as Parties Dispute Growth and Environmental Protections
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The new planning laws will shape how homes, infrastructure, energy projects and other developments are approved, with consequences for communities and the environment.
topicSummaries.content: The House passed legislation replacing the Resource Management Act with a new planning system the previous night. Reform Minister Chris Bishop said the changes would consolidate about 100 planning documents into 17 regional plans and could remove around 45 percent of current consent and permit requirements; he also cited projected economic benefits and $294 million in implementation funding over four years. Green co-leader Marama Davidson argued that the Government’s environmental and resource policies weakened protections, while Luxon said the Government would protect the environment and support growth and jobs. Implementation of the new system is expected to take several years.

keyExchanges.speaker: Marama Davidson (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: What is his message to the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who took to the streets in Auckland on Saturday, marching to demand environmental protections, who now see his Government dismantling decades of environmental protections?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I disagree. They’ve actually got a Government that will ensure the environment is protected, but, most importantly, they will grow and they will have jobs and opportunities for them and their families.

topicSummaries.topic: Māori Outcomes and Treaty Changes Remain a Major Political Divide
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Debates over Treaty obligations, Māori representation and services affect how public decisions are made and delivered for Māori communities.
topicSummaries.content: Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi challenged Luxon over the Government’s approach to Māori outcomes and changes to Māori authority in policy processes. Luxon defended the record by citing Treaty settlements advanced, families moved out of emergency housing, increased funding for Māori health providers and lower Māori youth offending. In closing speeches, Te Pāti Māori and Labour criticised changes to Treaty-related provisions and Māori representation, while ACT defended its position as equal treatment under the law. The exchanges underscored a continuing disagreement over whether the Government’s approach improves outcomes or reduces Māori influence and protections.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rawiri Waititi (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Why does the Prime Minister define success for Māori by counting how many Māori he has kicked out of emergency housing, how many Māori he has put into prison, and how many parents have been prosecuted to address attendance, rather than whether Māori have secure homes, decent incomes, good health, access to Māori-medium education, and genuine control over our own futures?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As I have said to the member repeatedly, we don’t believe in histrionics and performative stuff; we actually get things done in this Government. Just think about it: 18 Treaty Settlements advanced; a thousand-plus Māori families out of emergency housing, 80 percent reduction; Māori health provider funding nearly doubled over this Government.

topicSummaries.topic: New Zealand-India Trade Agreement Set to Take Effect on 20 October
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The agreement is intended to reduce tariffs and expand market access for New Zealand exporters selling goods and services in India.
topicSummaries.content: Trade and Investment Minister Nicola Grigg said New Zealand and India had formally ratified their free-trade agreement, which is scheduled to take effect on 20 October. She said 57 percent of current New Zealand exports to India would receive tariff-free access on the first day, rising to 82 percent once the agreement is fully implemented, with further reductions for other exports. Grigg identified forestry, wool, sheep meat and coal among the sectors benefiting immediately, and said tariffs on wine would fall in stages. The Government described the agreement as a significant opportunity for exporters; the transcript records no substantive opposition exchange on the deal.

keyExchanges.speaker: Carlos Cheung (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What progress has been made on the New Zealand-India free-trade agreement?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Grigg (National)
keyExchanges.quote: New Zealand and India now have formally ratified the New Zealand-India free-trade agreement (FTA). This is a significant milestone towards the implementation of one of New Zealand’s most significant agreements in decades.

topicSummaries.topic: Parliament Approves New Rules on Scrutiny and Urgency
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes will affect how bills are examined and how much time the public and MPs have to scrutinise legislation in the next Parliament.
topicSummaries.content: MPs unanimously approved amendments to the Standing Orders, the rules governing Parliament, for the next Parliament. The changes establish a Legislative Scrutiny Committee to examine broadly supported, non-controversial bills and require ministers to explain when legislation bypasses select-committee scrutiny or receives less than six months of consideration there. The rules also include changes to public engagement and the processing of submissions. Government and opposition members supported the package but differed over whether the new safeguards would sufficiently address concerns about urgency and shortened scrutiny.

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I do want to note that the committee has agreed to changes that I think will encourage a better use of urgency, including requiring Ministers to explain why they need to bypass select committee, and I hope that will help demonstrate that when urgency is used, it is for good reason.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tracey McLellan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: If a Government wants to remove an important stage of the parliamentary and public scrutiny, it is only fair and reasonable that they should at least have to explain why.

conclusion: The Parliament closed its term with major reforms passed and parliamentary rules updated, but the central contest over household costs, public services and the Government’s treatment of Māori and the environment now moves into the election campaign.
